chunks: "Brushes are the stationary contacts that deliver current to the spinning part of a brushed motor.

They're blocks of conductive material, usually carbon or graphite, in small motors sometimes thin metal fingers, held by springs against the commutator, which is a ring of copper segments on the rotor.
The motor's terminals connect to the brushes. They do two jobs.
First, they're the power connection: they let current flow from the fixed terminals into the windings of a rotating armature without a wire to twist.
Second, together with the commutator they do the switching.
As the rotor turns, each coil's segments pass under the brushes and the current in the coil reverses at the right angle.
That keeps the torque pointing the same way, so the motor keeps spinning in one direction instead of oscillating.
The downsides come from the fact that they slide on a moving surface. They wear, which limits life.
They have a contact voltage drop of roughly a volt for carbon brushes, so there's an I times V brush loss.
They make friction, and they spark a little at commutation, which makes electrical noise.
That's why brushless motors, which switch the current electronically and have no sliding contact, last longer and are quieter, at the cost of needing a controller."
